articles.title: FR-FCFS Explained: How Memory Controllers Pick the Next Command (and Why It Starves)
articles.excerpt: "How does a memory controller decide what to do next?" is a great interview question because it has no single right answer. But almost every answer starts from the same baseline: FR-FCFS. Here's how i…
articles.body: "How does a memory controller decide what to do next?" is a great interview question because it has no single right answer. But almost every answer starts from the same baseline: FR-FCFS . Here's how it works, the worked example interviewers like, and the flaw they'll ask you to fix. The problem a scheduler solves A DRAM bank can hold one open row at a time. A request to that open row (a hit ) only needs a column command. A request to a different row (a conflict ) needs a precharge, an activate, and then the column command, roughly three times the latency at DDR5-4800 (about 16.7 ns versus 48.7 ns to first data). So the order you serve requests in changes your bandwidth dramatically.

articles.title: Who turned the W upside down? Why Cassiopeia won't sit still
articles.excerpt: The queen in the northern night sky is supposedly one of the easiest constellations to recognize — you just look for a W. Or is that an M?
articles.body: Some constellations are like old friends. You know them well, they're always there, and they never seem to change. A case in point is Cassiopeia, the queen. Its beautiful name comes from Greek mythology — the mother of Andromeda — and its shape is said to represent a queen sitting on a throne. To a stargazer, Cassiopeia is best known as a prominent northern constellation shaped like the letter W. It's easy to find — look north, find five reasonably bright stars making a W, congratulate yourself on finding Cassiopeia and use it to get somewhere more interesting. It's so often a signpost, not a destination. But look north a few hours after dark this month, and you'll notice the W has gone.

articles.title: On this day in space! Nov. 27, 1885: Astronomer captures 1st known photo of a meteor during an Andromedid meteor storm
articles.excerpt: On Nov. 27, 1885, an astronomer made the first known photograph of a meteor. Here's why it mattered.
articles.body: On Nov. 27, 1885, an astronomer made the first known photograph of a meteor. The picture was taken by Austro-Hungarian astronomer Ladislaus Weinek. He captured the trail of the meteor on a photographic plate in the Czech Republic. The meteor he captured was part of the Andromedid meteor shower . The Andromedids were associated with Biela's Comet , which broke apart in the 1850s. When Weinek observed the meteor shower in 1885, it was in the middle of a meteor storm . This means that there were way more meteors than usual. Skywatchers could see thousands of meteors per hour. The November 1872 incidence of the Andromedid meteor shower, as seen over France, in a painting.

articles.body: NASA's Artemis III astronauts pose holding up three fingers to symbolize their mission as they visit the Orion spacecraft they will ride to space. (Image credit: NASA/Kim Shiflett) Training for a mission to space is hard work. But sometimes you have to take a minute and have a little fun with your crewmates. What is it? Crowded together with the Orion spacecraft, the four astronauts that make up the Artemis III crew hold up three fingers, taking a brief pause in their rigorous training for some lighthearted crew bonding.
